jdso8u-d1e76-d1e104.summary: Editorial title of the first prologue question: whether, in the present state, it is necessary for man that some special doctrine be supernaturally inspired that he could not reach by the natural light of the intellect.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e127.summary: First argument for the negative: a power with a common first natural object can naturally attain whatever falls under that object, as shown by induction and because a first object is by definition adequate to its power. The first natural object of our intellect is being as being (supported by Avicenna's claim that being and thing are impressed first on the soul); so the intellect can naturally know any being, any intelligible, even non-being through affirmation. No supernatural doctrine is needed.
claims: A power can naturally attain whatever falls under its adequate first object.
Being as being is the first natural object of the human intellect.
Therefore the intellect can naturally know every intelligible.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e201.summary: Second argument for the negative: sense needs no comparable supernatural knowledge, so neither does intellect. Nature does not fail in necessary things (De anima III), and if it does not fail the lower powers with respect to what they need for their acts and ends, still less does it fail the higher power.
claims: Sense requires no supernatural cognition.
Nature does not fail in what is necessary, a fortiori for higher powers.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e236.summary: Third argument for the negative, by infinite regress: if supernatural doctrine were needed, it would be because the intellect in its pure natural state is disproportioned to its object and must be proportioned by something else. If that something is natural, the whole remains disproportioned; if supernatural, the power is disproportioned to it in turn and needs a further proportioning, ad infinitum. So one must stop at the start: the intellect is of itself proportioned to every knowable in every mode.
claims: Requiring something to proportion the intellect to its object leads to infinite regress.
So the intellect must be naturally proportioned to every knowable.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e285.summary: Arguments for the affirmative from Scripture: 2 Timothy 3 (all Scripture is divinely inspired and useful for teaching), and Baruch 3, that only the one who knows all things knows the way of wisdom, which shows the necessity of revelation, and that he gave it to Jacob and later appeared on earth among men, which marks the actual giving in the Old and New Testaments.
claims: Wisdom necessary for salvation can come only from the one who knows all things.
God has in fact given it, in the Old and New Testaments.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e331.summary: Scotus frames the question as a controversy between philosophers, who hold the perfection of nature and deny supernatural perfection, and theologians, who recognize nature's defect and the need for grace. The philosopher would say no supernatural knowledge is necessary since all can be acquired from natural causes. The first philosophical argument is from De anima III: given the agent intellect, which makes all things, and the possible intellect, which becomes all things, both naturally present and unimpeded, and given that natural actives and passives suitably approximated necessarily act, the intellect can naturally understand any intelligible.
claims: Philosophers affirm the perfection of nature; theologians affirm its defect and the need for grace.
An unimpeded natural active and passive principle, suitably approximated, necessarily produce their action.
The agent and possible intellects are natural principles sufficient for knowing any intelligible.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e412.summary: Confirmation of the philosophers' argument: every natural passive power has a corresponding natural active power, otherwise it would be in vain in nature. The possible intellect is naturally passive towards every intelligible, since it naturally desires and is naturally perfected by every cognition; so it has a natural active counterpart for every intelligible.
claims: Every natural passive power has a corresponding natural active power.
The possible intellect is naturally receptive of every intellection.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e454.summary: Second philosophical argument: Metaphysics VI divides speculative science into metaphysics, physics and mathematics, and the reasoning there seems to exclude any further speculative science, since these together cover all of being in itself and in its parts. Likewise there is no practical science beyond the acquired practical sciences of action and making. So acquired sciences suffice to perfect both speculative and practical intellect.
claims: Metaphysics, physics and mathematics exhaust speculative science.
Acquired practical sciences exhaust practical science.
Acquired sciences suffice to perfect the intellect.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e499.summary: Third philosophical argument: whoever can naturally know a principle can naturally know the conclusions it contains, since science of conclusions depends only on understanding the principle and on deduction, which is self-evident as perfect syllogism. We naturally understand first principles, which virtually contain all knowable conclusions, so we can naturally know them all.
claims: Knowing a principle naturally enables knowing its conclusions naturally.
Syllogistic deduction is evident of itself.
First principles, naturally known, virtually contain all knowable conclusions.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e565.summary: Proof of the minor of the third argument: the terms of first principles are the most common, which we understand first (Physics I), and we know principles by knowing their terms, so we can naturally know first principles. And since such terms, taken universally in first principles, extend to all lower concepts, they reach the terms of all particular conclusions.
claims: The terms of first principles are the most common and are naturally understood first.
Universally taken, these terms extend to all particular concepts and conclusions.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e617.summary: First of three arguments against the philosophers' position: every agent acting through cognition needs distinct knowledge of its end, since every per se agent acts for an end from appetite for it, and in a cognitive agent appetite follows cognition. Man cannot naturally know his end distinctly. Proof: Aristotle, following natural reason, either places happiness in acquired knowledge of separate substances or at least concludes nothing higher, so natural reason either errs about the end in particular or stays in doubt, as Aristotle's hesitant remark about happiness as a gift of the gods (Ethics I) shows.
claims: Every cognitive agent needs distinct knowledge of its end.
Man cannot know his end distinctly by natural reason.
Aristotle either erred about the particular end or remained in doubt about it.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e710.summary: Second proof that man cannot naturally know his end: we know the proper end of a substance only from its manifest acts that show the end suits its nature, and in this life we experience no acts showing that vision of separate substances suits us. At least certain conditions of the end that make it more desirable cannot be concluded naturally: even if reason showed that the vision and enjoyment of God is man's end, it would not conclude that it belongs perpetually to the whole person in body and soul (see IV d.43), though perpetuity and bodily integrity make it more desirable. Such conditions must be known to seek the end effectively, so supernatural doctrine is required.
claims: A substance's proper end is known only from its manifest acts.
No acts in this life show that vision of separate substances suits our nature.
Natural reason cannot establish the perpetuity of beatitude or that it belongs to body and soul together.
These conditions make the end more desirable and are needed for effective pursuit.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e806.summary: Second argument against the philosophers: every knowing agent acting for an end needs three cognitions: how the end is attained, all things necessary for it, and that these suffice. Without the first it cannot dispose itself; without the second it may fail through ignorance of something necessary; without the third it will pursue the necessary without conviction, fearing something is lacking.
claims: A cognitive agent needs to know how the end is attained, what is necessary for it, and that this suffices.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e858.summary: The wayfarer cannot know these three by natural reason. Beatitude is given as a reward for merits to one whom God accepts as worthy, so it follows from our acts by no natural necessity but contingently through God's acceptance of certain acts as meritorious. This is not naturally knowable, as the philosophers' error of holding that whatever God does immediately he does necessarily shows. The other two, what God accepts and that it suffices, depend purely on the divine will in matters where it acts contingently.
claims: Beatitude is a reward given contingently by divine acceptance of acts as meritorious, not a natural consequence of acts.
Philosophers erred in holding that all God's immediate effects are necessary.
What God accepts as meritorious and its sufficiency depend on his contingent will, which reason cannot know.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e918.summary: Objection to the first argument: every created nature depends essentially on each of its per se causes, so from knowing the effect each such cause can be known by demonstration quia. Since human nature is naturally knowable to us, its end can be known from it. This holds for lower natures and should hold here too. It also seems to falsify the premiss that a substance's end is known only from its acts, since the end can be known from the nature in itself.
claims: From a known effect its per se causes, including the final cause, can be known by demonstration quia.
Human nature is naturally knowable, so its end can be naturally known.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e982.summary: Reply to a possible defence that only the natural, not supernatural, end can be known: Augustine (De praedestinatione sanctorum) says that the ability to have faith and charity belongs to human nature, while having them belongs to grace. If human nature is naturally knowable, so is this capacity and thus the ordering of nature to the end for which faith and charity dispose.
claims: The capacity for faith and charity belongs to human nature (Augustine).
If human nature is naturally knowable, so is its ordering to the end to which faith and charity dispose.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1024.summary: Further objections: man naturally desires this so-called supernatural end, so he is naturally ordered to it and it can be known from his nature. Also, it is naturally knowable (per Avicenna) that being is the first object of the intellect and that being is most perfectly realized in God; the end of any power is the best within its first object, in which alone is perfect rest and delight (Ethics X); so it is naturally knowable that man is ordered to God as end.
claims: Man naturally desires his supernatural end.
Being is naturally known to be the first object of the intellect.
The end of a power is the best thing within its first object, which is God for the intellect.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1070.summary: Confirmation: whoever naturally knows a power knows its first object and what most perfectly realizes it, which is its end. The mind is known to itself (Augustine, De Trinitate XIV), so it knows its first object and that God does not exceed it, since otherwise God would be unintelligible; so it knows God as the best realization of its object and the end of the power.
claims: Knowing a power entails knowing its first object and its most perfect instance.
The mind knows itself, so knows God as the end of its intellectual power.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1123.summary: Objection to the second argument: if one extreme is known through the other, so is the middle. The things necessary to attain the end are means between nature and end; since the end is knowable from nature, so are the means. As in other cases, the necessary connection of means to end allows inferring the means from the end, as what health requires is inferred from the notion of health.
claims: If nature and end are known, the necessary means between them can be known.
Means are inferred from ends by their necessary connection.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1171.summary: Scotus's single reply to the objection from per se causes, the Augustinian text, and the argument from the first object (noting the first concerns the end as final cause, not as attained by operation). All assume that our nature or intellect is naturally knowable to us. This is false under the proper and special ratio by which it is ordered to this end, is capable of consummate grace, and has God as its most perfect object. In this life we know the soul and our nature only under general rationes abstractable from sensibles (see d.3 q.3), and under those it is not ordered to this end, nor capable of grace, nor has God as most perfect object.
claims: In this life we know our nature only under general concepts abstracted from sensibles.
We do not know our nature under the special ratio by which it is ordered to its supernatural end and capable of grace.
So the end cannot be inferred from our knowledge of our nature.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1235.summary: Applied to the form of the argument: the end can be known by demonstration quia from a being ordered to it only if that being is known under the proper ratio by which it has the end, and so the minor is false. As for proportionality, though the mind is the same as itself, in this life it is proportioned to itself as object only under general rationes abstractable from imaginable things.
claims: Demonstration quia of an end requires knowing the being under its proper ratio.
In this life the mind is an object to itself only under general concepts.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1268.summary: Reply to the confirmation: the proper ends of other substances are not known either, except where manifest acts show their ordering. So the premiss that a substance's proper end is known only through its manifest acts stands; it does not deny other ways in principle. If a substance were known under its proper ratio, its per se cause could be demonstrated quia, but no substance is so known now, so we can conclude its proper end only from evident acts of it, known universally and confusedly.
claims: Proper ends of substances are known only through manifest acts, given how we now know substances.
Were a substance known under its proper ratio, its end could be demonstrated from it, but this is not our present condition.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1333.summary: In the present case both ways to knowing the end fail: we know neither our nature under its proper ratio nor acts that reveal the end. The earlier proof explicitly used ignorance of acts while presupposing ignorance of the nature itself.
claims: We lack both knowledge of our nature under its proper ratio and knowledge of acts revealing our end.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1346.summary: Reply to the Augustinian argument: the capacity for charity, as a disposition toward God under the proper ratio of lovability, belongs to human nature under a special ratio not shared with sensibles, so it is not naturally knowable. Against the distinction of natural and supernatural ends, Scotus concedes that God is man's natural end, though to be attained supernaturally, not naturally; the argument from natural desire proves this, and he grants it.
claims: The capacity for charity belongs to human nature under a special ratio not naturally known.
God is man's natural end, though attainable only supernaturally.
Man has a natural desire for God.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1401.summary: Reply to the argument from the first object: it is false that we naturally know being to be the first object of our intellect in its full indifference to sensibles and insensibles. Avicenna's claim does not show this is naturally known, for he mixed his religion (Islam) with philosophy, saying some things as proven by reason and others as consonant with his religion; thus he holds that the separated soul knows immaterial substance in itself and so must include it under the intellect's first object. Aristotle did not; for him the first object seems to be the quiddity of a sensible thing, or one abstractable from sensibles.
claims: It is not naturally known that being, indifferent to sensible and insensible, is the first object of our intellect.
Avicenna's view reflects religious commitments mixed with philosophy.
For Aristotle the first object of our intellect is the quiddity of sensible things.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1462.summary: An addition (Additio) raises an objection: if the quiddity of material things were the adequate object of the intellect, it could know nothing of separate substances, since the adequate object contains formally or virtually all a power can reach. Reply: the premiss is false, for the five common sensibles (number, figure, motion, magnitude, rest) are seen per se though contained neither formally nor virtually under light or color; some agreement or concomitance suffices.
claims: A power can attain things not contained formally or virtually under its adequate object.
The common sensibles are seen per se though not contained under color or light.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1503.summary: Reply to the Augustinian confirmation that the mind is known to itself: Augustine's statement concerns first act, which of itself suffices for second act, but is now impeded, so the second act (actual self-knowledge) is not elicited; more on this later.
claims: The mind's self-presence is a first act sufficient for self-knowledge, but in this state its second act is impeded.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1532.summary: Objection to Scotus's reply: in the state of innocence man could know his nature and so, by the first argument's reasoning, his end; so this knowledge is not supernatural.
claims: In the state of innocence man could know his nature and hence his end.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1548.summary: Another objection to the reply about the first object: if we cannot know the intellect's first object because we do not know the intellect under its proper ratio, then we cannot know of anything that it is intelligible, since we do not know the power under the ratio by which it relates to anything as intelligible.
claims: If the first object is unknowable for this reason, nothing could be known to be intelligible.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1577.summary: Reply to the objection from the state of innocence: what knowledge man had as first instituted is deferred, but at least for the wayfarer in the present state this knowledge is supernatural, since it exceeds his natural capacity, 'natural' being taken according to the state of fallen nature.
claims: For the present wayfarer, knowledge of the end exceeds natural capacity as it stands in fallen nature.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1599.summary: Reply to the objection about the first object: Scotus grants that we do not now know the soul or its powers so distinctly as to infer their objects from them. Rather, from acts we experience we infer the power and nature whose act it is, and that its object includes what we perceive the act to attain; the object is concluded from the experienced act, not from knowledge of the power. For a supernatural object we have neither kind of knowledge, so both ways of knowing the proper end fail.
claims: We infer powers and their objects from experienced acts, not the other way round.
For a supernatural object we have neither knowledge of the power under its proper ratio nor experienced acts.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1645.summary: Reply to the objection against the second argument: it presupposes what has been denied, that the end is naturally knowable. To its confirmation: means can be concluded from the end only when the end follows naturally from the means and naturally requires them. Here the connection is not natural but depends solely on the divine will accepting merits as worthy of the end.
claims: Means can be inferred from an end only when the end follows naturally from them.
The link between merits and beatitude is divine acceptance, not natural consequence.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1679.summary: Third argument against the philosophers, from Metaphysics VI: knowledge of separate substances is the noblest, so knowledge of what is proper to them is most noble and necessary, being more perfect than what they share with sensibles. But we cannot know these proper features naturally. If any natural science taught them, it would be metaphysics, yet metaphysics cannot, first because they are not virtually contained in its first subject, being; as Aristotle says (Metaphysics I), the wise man (the metaphysician) knows all things somehow, universally rather than in particular.
claims: Knowledge of what is proper to separate substances is most noble and necessary.
No natural science, not even metaphysics, can teach these proper features.
Proper features of separate substances are not virtually contained in being, the subject of metaphysics.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1759.summary: Second proof: such proper features cannot be known by demonstration propter quid without knowing their proper subjects, which are not naturally knowable to us. Nor by demonstration quia from effects, since effects either leave the mind in doubt or mislead it. Example: a proper feature of the divine nature is to be communicable to three persons, but effects do not show this, since they are not from God as triune.
claims: Propter quid knowledge of proper features requires knowledge of their proper subjects, which we lack.
Effects do not reveal the proper features of separate substances.
Creatures do not manifest the Trinity, since they are not from God as triune.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1805.summary: Arguing from effects to cause actually leads to error: no effect exhibits one numerical nature except in one supposit, which suggests the opposite of the Trinity. Similarly, the divine nature's property ad extra is to cause contingently, but effects lead rather to the opposite error, as philosophers who held the first cause acts necessarily show.
claims: Effects suggest that one nature exists in one supposit, contrary to the Trinity.
God causes contingently, but reasoning from effects led philosophers to think he causes necessarily.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1834.summary: The same holds for other separate substances: effects point more to their sempiternity, eternity and necessity than to their contingency and novelty. Philosophers inferred their number from the number of celestial motions, and held them naturally blessed and impeccable, all of which Scotus judges utterly absurd.
claims: Reasoning from effects leads to false conclusions about separate substances (eternity, necessity, number, impeccability).

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1877.summary: Objection to the third argument: whatever necessary truths about separate substances we now know by faith or common revelation can be known naturally.
claims: All revealed necessary truths about separate substances can be known naturally.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1895.summary: Proof of the objection: if we naturally know the terms of any revealed necessary truth, we can naturally grasp it. If immediate, it is known once its terms are known; if mediate, since we can know the extremes we can conceive a middle term and proceed until we reach immediate truths from which the mediate follow. And we do naturally know the terms of all revealed truths, since believer and unbeliever contradict each other about concepts, not merely words, as when philosopher and theologian disagree about 'God is triune'.
claims: Whoever knows the terms of a necessary truth can, through middle terms, reach its evidence.
Believers and unbelievers share the same concepts when they disagree about revealed propositions.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e1987.summary: Reply: there are immediate truths about separate substances (say A), containing many mediate truths (B, C) that predicate common features of common subjects. These mediate truths have evidence only from the immediate truth A. An intellect that can grasp and compose the terms of B and C but not those of A finds B and C neutral, neither evident nor refutable. So it is with us: we have common concepts of immaterial and material substances and can compose them, but these compositions get their evidence only from immediate truths about those quiddities under their proper ratio, which we do not conceive.
claims: Mediate truths about separate substances have evidence only from immediate truths about their proper quiddities.
We have only common concepts of these substances, so the relevant propositions remain neutral to us.
Ability to form a proposition does not entail ability to know its truth.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2059.summary: Illustration: someone unable to conceive a triangle under its proper ratio could still abstract the concept of figure from a quadrangle and primacy from numbers, and so form 'some figure is first'. But this proposition would remain neutral to him, since it is mediate, contained in the immediate 'the triangle is first in this way', whose terms he cannot grasp.
claims: One can form a proposition from common concepts while its evidence depends on an immediate truth one cannot grasp.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2118.summary: Reply to the form of the objection: deny the major. The truths are mediate, and the inference 'we can know the extremes, so we can conceive the middle' fails, because the middle sometimes is essentially ordered between the extremes, such as the definition of one extreme or a prior property relative to a later one, which is the kind of middle that concludes one extreme of the other universally.
claims: Knowing the extremes of a mediate truth does not ensure ability to conceive its middle term.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2151.summary: Scotus concedes that anyone who can grasp the extremes can grasp an essentially ordered middle, since it is included in or identical with one of the extremes. But if the middle is a particular contained under one extreme and not essentially ordered, then one who can conceive general extremes need not be able to conceive the particular middle. So here: the quiddity under its proper ratio is a lower middle that concludes the property of the common concept only particularly, as the triangle is a middle for concluding primacy of figure only particularly.
claims: An essentially ordered middle is accessible to anyone who grasps the extremes.
A particular middle under a general extreme need not be accessible from general concepts.
Proper quiddities of separate substances are such particular middles.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2229.summary: The third argument applies above all to the first immaterial substance, God, knowledge of whom as beatific object is most necessary. The reply presupposes that we now conceive God naturally only in a general concept common to him and sensibles (to be explained in d.3 q.1). Even if that is denied, a concept of God formed by virtue of creatures is imperfect, while one caused by the divine essence itself would be perfect; so the same reply holds in terms of imperfect and perfect concepts instead of general and special ones.
claims: The argument applies chiefly to God as beatific object.
Naturally we conceive God only in a concept common to him and creatures.
A concept of God caused by creatures is imperfect compared to one caused by the divine essence.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2281.summary: Objection to the main conclusion: suppose an unbaptized adult with no teacher who does all the good he can according to right natural reason and avoids what reason shows to be evil. Even if God ordinarily visits such a person with a teacher (as with Cornelius), suppose he is not taught: he will be saved, and indeed is already just and worthy of eternal life through good willing that merits grace, yet he has no theology, not even the first articles of faith, only natural knowledge. So nothing theological is strictly necessary for salvation.
claims: An untaught, unbaptized adult who follows right reason could be saved.
Such a person would have only natural knowledge, not theology.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2329.summary: Reply: such a person, by good willing, merits de congruo justification from original sin, and God, not bound to the sacraments, gives first grace without a sacrament. Grace is not given without the habit of theological faith, though it cannot issue in act without instruction, just as with the baptized infant; though not contradictory, simultaneous infusion can be posited as in baptism. By absolute power God could save anyone, even merit without infused faith; but by ordained power grace is not infused without faith, not because grace needs it but from divine liberality reforming the whole person. Theology, whose perfect habit includes infused and acquired faith together, is thus necessary by ordained power as to infused faith, for all; acquired faith is perhaps necessary for adults who can have and understand a teacher.
claims: God, not bound to sacraments, can justify the well-disposed without them, merit de congruo preceding.
By ordained power grace is always infused with the habit of faith.
By absolute power God could save without infused faith.
Infused faith is necessary for all by ordained power; acquired faith perhaps for adults with access to a teacher.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2452.summary: A fourth argument (Henry of Ghent's): what is ordered to an end for which it is of itself undisposed must be gradually disposed; man is ordered to a supernatural end for which he is undisposed, so he needs gradual disposition through some supernatural knowledge. If a perfect agent could remove imperfection at once, still it is more perfect to give man some activity in reaching his perfection, which requires imperfect knowledge preceding the perfect knowledge to which he is ordered.
claims: What is undisposed for its end must be gradually disposed.
It is more perfect for man to share actively in reaching his end, which requires prior imperfect knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2516.summary: A fifth argument (Henry of Ghent's): an agent using an instrument cannot through it perform an action exceeding the instrument's nature. The agent intellect's light is the instrument the soul now uses in natural knowing, and it is limited to knowledge via the senses; so the soul cannot naturally know what cannot be known through the senses, yet much such knowledge is necessary now.
claims: An instrument cannot produce an action exceeding its nature.
The agent intellect's light is limited to sense-derived knowledge.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2558.summary: Scotus turns the fifth argument against its author: on Henry's account, uncreated light could not use the agent intellect as an instrument for knowing pure truth, since that cannot be had through the senses without special illumination; then the agent intellect would have no role in knowing pure truth, which is absurd, since this is the more perfect act and the soul's more perfect intellectual principle should concur in it.
claims: The instrument argument would exclude the agent intellect from knowing pure truth, which Henry himself would reject.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2602.summary: Scotus judges these two arguments ineffective. The first would work only if it were proven that man is finally ordered to supernatural knowledge (a matter for the questions on beatitude) and that natural knowledge does not sufficiently dispose for it now. The second assumes two things: that knowledge of things not knowable through the senses is necessary, and that the agent intellect's light is limited to such things. So the first three arguments are more probable.
claims: Henry's gradual-disposition argument presupposes unproven premisses.
The instrument argument assumes the agent intellect is limited to sense-knowable objects.
The first three arguments against the philosophers are more probable.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2653.summary: Scotus's own answer begins by distinguishing senses of 'supernatural'. A receptive power can be compared to the act it receives or to the agent from which it receives it. In the first comparison it is natural (naturally inclined to the form), violent (against its inclination), or neutral, and here there is no supernaturality at all.
claims: A receptive power's relation to its received act is natural, violent or neutral, never supernatural.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2689.summary: In the second comparison, receptive power to agent, there is naturality when the agent is naturally apt to impress that form in that patient, and supernaturality when it is not.
claims: Supernaturality lies in the relation of receiver to an agent that is not naturally apt to produce that form in it.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2713.summary: Applied: compared to its act, no knowledge is supernatural for the possible intellect, which is naturally perfected by and inclined to any cognition. Compared to its agent, knowledge is supernatural when produced by an agent not naturally apt to move the possible intellect to it. In this state, per Aristotle, the possible intellect is naturally moved by the agent intellect and phantasm, so only what they can impress is natural. They suffice for all simple (incomplex) knowledge the wayfarer ordinarily has, so although God can cause simple knowledge by special revelation (as in rapture), such knowledge is not necessary by the common law.
claims: No cognition is supernatural for the possible intellect in relation to its act.
Cognition is supernatural when caused by an agent not naturally apt to move the intellect to it.
In this state only the agent intellect and phantasm are natural movers of the intellect.
Supernatural knowledge of simple terms is not necessary by common law.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2787.summary: With complex truths it is otherwise: as the three arguments showed, even with the full action of agent intellect and phantasms, many propositions we need to know remain unknown and neutral. Their knowledge must be handed down supernaturally, since no one could discover them naturally and teach others, for they are neutral to everyone alike.
claims: Many necessary complex truths remain neutral to natural cognition.
Such truths must be supernaturally handed down, since no one can naturally discover them.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2822.summary: Whether, after doctrine is first handed down, one can assent to it naturally is deferred to III d.23. The first handing down is called revelation, and it is supernatural because it comes from an agent that is not a natural mover of our intellect in this state.
claims: Revelation is supernatural because its agent is not a natural mover of our intellect in this state.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2846.summary: A second sense in which revelation is supernatural: it comes from an agent standing in for (supplying the role of) a supernatural object. The object naturally apt to cause knowledge of 'God is three and one' is the divine essence known under its proper ratio, which is supernatural for us. Whatever causes knowledge of truths that would be evident through that object supplies its role, perfectly if it causes knowledge as perfect as the object would, imperfectly if its knowledge is less perfect and virtually contained in the perfect.
claims: Revelation's agent supplies the role of the supernatural object, the divine essence under its proper ratio.
It does so perfectly or imperfectly depending on the knowledge it causes.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2910.summary: Application: the one revealing 'God is triune' causes in the mind some obscure knowledge of that truth, since it concerns an object not known under its proper ratio; if that object were known it would cause perfect and clear knowledge.
claims: Revelation of the Trinity produces obscure knowledge, because the object is not known under its proper ratio.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2932.summary: Since the obscure knowledge is eminently included in the clear as the imperfect in the perfect, the revealer supplies the role of the object causing the clear knowledge, especially because no agent can cause knowledge of a truth except by standing in for some object. Nor can it do so by standing in for a lower, naturally moving object, since none virtually includes even obscure knowledge of these truths. So even in causing obscure knowledge it supplies the role of a supernatural object.
claims: Any agent causes knowledge of a truth only by supplying the role of some object.
No natural object virtually includes even obscure knowledge of revealed truths about God.
So revelation, even when obscure, supplies the role of a supernatural object.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e2978.summary: The two senses of 'supernatural' are distinguished by separating them: if a supernatural agent infused knowledge of a natural object (e.g. geometry), it would be supernatural in the first sense (from an agent not naturally apt to cause it) but not the second (supplying a supernatural object). Infused knowledge of 'God is triune' would be supernatural in both senses, since the second entails the first but not conversely. Knowledge supernatural only in the first sense could be had naturally; knowledge supernatural in the second sense can only be had supernaturally.
claims: Supernaturality by agent does not entail supernaturality by object, but the converse holds.
Knowledge supernatural by object can only be had supernaturally.
Infused geometry would be supernatural only by agent.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3032.summary: The first two of the three arguments supporting the solution are confirmed by Augustine: philosophers, not knowing to what end things should be referred, saw some truth amid falsehood (City of God XVIII); and what use is knowing where to go if one does not know the way (City of God II)? Philosophers mixed falsehood with truths about virtue, as Aristotle shows of others' constitutions (Politics II), while his own is not blameless: he teaches honoring the gods, forbids rearing deformed infants, and prescribes abortion in certain cases (Politics VII).
claims: Philosophers did not know the end to which things should be referred.
Knowing the end is useless without knowing the way.
Philosophical ethics, including Aristotle's, mixes truth with error.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3128.summary: The third argument is confirmed by Augustine (City of God XI.3): for what is beyond our senses we need other witnesses. This confirms the whole solution: since the relevant propositions are neutral to us, no one can believe them on his own testimony; supernatural testimony from someone above the whole human species is required. How the first revelation came about, by inner or outer speech, with signs sufficient to cause assent, is uncertain; it suffices that it could be revealed either way supernaturally but could not first be handed down by a human without error.
claims: What lies beyond our senses must be known by testimony.
The testimony needed for neutral truths must come from someone above the human species.
The mode of first revelation is uncertain, but it could not originate from a human without error.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3189.summary: Objection that the three arguments are self-defeating: what is shown necessary to know is thereby shown true, since only truth is known. So whatever they show necessary (that enjoyment of God is man's end, that the way is merit accepted by God, that God is triune and causes contingently) is shown true. Either the arguments rest only on faith, or they conclude the opposite of what they set out to prove (that these truths cannot be known naturally).
claims: Showing something must be known shows it to be true.
So the arguments either presuppose faith or naturally prove what they say cannot be naturally known.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3237.summary: Reply: natural reason shows that it is necessary to know determinately one side of a contradiction (enjoyment is the end, or is not), so that the intellect is not merely doubtful or neutral, since such doubt would impede attaining the end. It does not show that this particular side must be known. As natural, the arguments conclude only to one side or the other indeterminately; they conclude to this side determinately only from what is believed.
claims: Natural reason shows the need to know determinately one side of certain contradictions, not which side.
The arguments, as natural, establish the need for revelation without establishing its content.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3278.summary: Reply to the philosophers' first argument: cognition depends on both the knowing soul and the known object (Augustine, De Trinitate IX). The soul has within itself sufficient active and passive principles insofar as the action of knowing belongs to the soul, but not insofar as it belongs to the object, for in that respect the soul is a blank tablet (De anima III). Aristotle's dictum that the agent intellect makes all things holds of the soul's share in cognition, not of the object's.
claims: Cognition is produced by both knower and object.
The soul lacks within itself the activity that belongs to the object.
The agent intellect's universal activity concerns the soul's part in cognition only.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3334.summary: Reply to the confirmation (every natural passive power has a natural active counterpart), distinguishing two senses of nature: an intrinsic principle of motion or rest (Physics II), or a principle acting naturally as opposed to art or will. In the first sense the major is false, since many things are naturally receptive of perfections without an intrinsic active principle. In the second sense it fails where a nature, by its excellence, is ordered to receive a perfection so eminent that no natural agent can cause it, as here. The passive power is not in vain, since a natural agent can dispose for it and some other agent within the whole order of beings, a supernatural one, can bring it to completion.
claims: Not every natural passive power has a corresponding natural active principle.
An excellent nature can be naturally receptive of a perfection no natural agent can produce.
Such a passive power is not in vain, since a supernatural agent can actualize it.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3424.summary: Objection: this disparages nature, since nature fails less in nobler things (De caelo II). Reply: if happiness consisted in the highest speculation we can naturally reach, the philosopher would not say nature fails; Scotus grants that this is naturally attainable and adds that a still more eminent perfection can be naturally received. This dignifies nature more than holding that its highest possibility is merely natural. It is no wonder that a nature's passive capacity extends further than its active causality.
claims: Natural capacity for a supernatural perfection dignifies nature rather than disparaging it.
A nature's passive capacity can exceed its active causality.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3478.summary: The De caelo text is not relevant: Aristotle says nature would have given stars organs if they had motive power. Scotus grants that whatever has an organic power is given an organ by nature (barring deformity). But here a non-organic power is given, and not everything that concurs in its act besides the power is given naturally. Aristotle shows only that what is naturally ordered to an act or object has the power, and the organ if organic, not all posterior requisites.
claims: Nature supplies the power and its organ, not all later requisites for the act.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3532.summary: An alternative reply: the major is true of a natural passive power as compared to the active power, not as compared to the received act; the distinction was drawn at the start of the solution. The minor is true in the second sense, not the first.
claims: The correspondence principle holds for passive power relative to its agent, not to its received act.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3556.summary: A third, easier reply denies the minor: though the possible intellect is absolutely naturally receptive of such intellection, it is not so in the present state, for reasons given in d.3 qq.1-3.
claims: The possible intellect is absolutely, but not in the present state, naturally receptive of such intellection.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3576.summary: A reply given to the second philosophical argument (the sufficiency of the speculative sciences): a different formal ratio of the knowable makes a different science, as astronomer and natural philosopher both demonstrate that the earth is round, one by a mathematical middle, the other by a physical one. So nothing prevents another science treating the same things the philosophical sciences treat, insofar as they are known by the light of divine revelation (the Thomist position).
claims: A different formal ratio of knowability distinguishes sciences even about the same things.
Theology can treat the same things as philosophy under the light of revelation.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3620.summary: Against that reply: if knowledge of theology's objects can be given in other sciences under another light, theological knowledge of them is not necessary, as one who knows the earth is round by a physical middle does not need the mathematical one. A defence follows: a habit, as habit, is distinguished by its object; as form, by its active principle; and principles are effective causes of scientific habits. So where the knowable is the same there is still distinction by the principles, and the habits are distinct as forms.
claims: If theological objects can be known by another science, theology is not necessary for them.
A defence distinguishes habits as forms by their principles even when objects are the same.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3682.summary: Against the defence: form is more common than habit, since every habit is a form but not conversely. Things cannot be distinct under the higher ratio and indistinct under the lower, so they cannot be distinct as forms yet indistinct as habits; that is like being distinct as animals and not as men.
claims: What is indistinct under a lower ratio is indistinct under a higher one.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3713.summary: Further, the defence wrongly supposes that principles distinguish the habit of the conclusion in some other causal mode than as effective principles. And the argument stands regardless: however many distinct habits one posits, one habit is not thereby shown necessary if another, distinct in whatever way, could give the knowledge. Scotus's own reply: the speculative sciences deal with all speculables, but not with everything knowable about them, specifically not their proper features, as the third main argument showed.
claims: Principles distinguish habits only as effective causes.
Positing distinct habits does not prove the necessity of any one.
Philosophical sciences cover all things but not all that is knowable about them, notably their proper features.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3776.summary: A reply given to the third philosophical argument (first principles virtually contain all conclusions): first principles can be applied only to sensible conclusions, both because their terms are abstracted from sensibles and savor of their nature, and because the agent intellect, which must apply them, is limited to sensibles.
claims: First principles apply only to sensible matters, on this view, because their terms and the agent intellect are limited to the sensible.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3803.summary: Against that reply: the intellect is certain that first principles are true of the insensible as well as the sensible; we no more doubt that contradictories are not true together of the immaterial than of the material. Nor does it help to say that the term of the first principle is being divided into ten categories, which does not reach the theological object, since we no more doubt that God is not both blessed and not blessed.
claims: First principles, such as non-contradiction, are known to hold of immaterial beings and of God.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3840.summary: Another reply: conclusions do not follow from major premisses alone but with minors added, and the needed minors are not naturally evident. Against: the minors under first principles predicate their terms of what falls under the subject terms of the first principles, and those terms, being most common, are known to be said of anything.
claims: Conclusions require minor premisses as well as first principles.
Against this, the minors would be known since the terms of first principles apply to everything.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3872.summary: Scotus's own reply: the second part of the minor is false, that first principles virtually contain all knowable conclusions. Subject and predicate terms of first principles are both common; when the distributed subject is taken for all things, it is only with respect to the most common predicates. So by such principles only the most common predicates are known of lower things.
claims: First principles do not virtually contain all knowable conclusions.
Through first principles only the most common predicates can be known of particular things.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3909.summary: Proof: a middle can be the reason why (propter quid) only for a property virtually included in its ratio. The subject of a most common principle includes only the most common properties, not particular ones; so it can be the means of knowing only those. Since there are many other knowable properties, there are many knowable truths not included in first principles.
claims: A middle term demonstrates only properties virtually included in its ratio.
The common subject of first principles includes only the most common properties.
So many knowable truths are not included in first principles.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3951.summary: Example: 'every whole is greater than its part' includes 'four is greater than two' and similar truths with the same predicate, but not 'four is double two' or 'three is sesquialter to two'; these predicates require special middles.
claims: A common principle includes particular truths only with the same predicate.
Particular predicates require special middle terms.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e3977.summary: A second, logical reason: in a universal affirmative one may descend under the subject but not under the predicate. Many predicates contained under those of first principles are knowable of things under their subjects, so these predicates are not known of those subjects through first principles.
claims: One can descend under the subject of a universal affirmative but not under its predicate.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4008.summary: Objection: from 'of anything, affirmation or negation is necessarily true' it follows necessarily that this is white or not white, so descent is possible under subject and predicate. Reply: the principle amounts to 'of any contradiction, one part is true and the other false', with a double distribution on the subject side under which descent is licit. But under a predicate standing merely confusedly, descent is not licit: one cannot infer 'therefore this part'. In all principles the predicate of a universal affirmative stands merely confusedly.
claims: The principle of excluded middle licenses descent under its distributed subjects but not under its predicate.
The predicate of a universal affirmative has merely confused supposition.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4065.summary: Illustration: it is true that man is risible, but from 'of anything, affirmation or negation' one can infer only that man is risible or not risible. Which side of the disjunction holds is never known through the common principle; a special principle is needed as the determinate middle and reason for knowing risibility of man.
claims: Common principles yield only disjunctions about particulars; a special principle is required to determine which side holds.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4097.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: 'natural object' can mean what a power can attain by the action of natural causes, or what it is naturally inclined to, whether or not it can naturally attain it. The major could be denied in the first sense: the first object is adequate to the power and abstracted from everything it acts on, and naturally understanding the common object does not entail naturally understanding everything under it, since understanding something contained is far more excellent than confused understanding of the common. So granting the minor in either sense, the intended conclusion does not follow.
claims: 'Natural object' means either what is naturally attainable or what the power is naturally inclined to.
Naturally knowing a common object does not entail naturally knowing everything under it.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4158.summary: Scotus argues that this reply defeats itself: the first object is by definition adequate, so the power regards as object all and only what has its ratio. It is impossible for something to be the natural first object without everything under it being a natural per se object; otherwise it would exceed the power and something lower would be adequate and first.
claims: If something is the natural adequate object, everything under it is a natural per se object of the power.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4195.summary: The reply's reasoning commits the fallacy of figure of speech: being as one intelligible grasped in one act (like man in one intellection) is naturally attainable, but being as first, adequate object is naturally attainable only if everything under it is. The inference from 'being is naturally attainable' to 'being as adequate object is naturally attainable' switches a 'this something' to a 'such a kind', since the antecedent concerns being as one singular intelligible and the consequent being as included in all intelligibles.
claims: Being as a single intelligible differs from being as adequate object included in all intelligibles.
Inferring the latter's natural attainability from the former's is a fallacy of figure of speech.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4260.summary: The real reply to the first argument: the minor is false of the natural object as what is naturally attainable, but true of the object to which the power is naturally inclined, and this is how Avicenna should be read; what the naturally attainable first object is is treated in d.3. Anselm confirms it (De libero arbitrio 2): we have no power that alone suffices for its act. So it is not unfitting that a power be naturally ordered to an object it cannot naturally attain, as any power is ordered to its act yet cannot attain it alone.
claims: Being is the first object to which the intellect is naturally inclined, not what it can naturally attain in this state.
A power can be naturally ordered to an object it cannot naturally attain.
No power alone suffices for its act (Anselm).

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4325.summary: Reply to the second principal argument (nature does not fail the intellect if it does not fail the senses): deny the consequence. Higher powers are ordered to receive passively a greater perfection than they can actively produce, which only a supernatural agent can produce; lower powers' ultimate perfection can fall under lower agents.
claims: Higher powers are ordered to perfections only a supernatural agent can produce.
Lower powers' perfections fall within the causality of natural agents.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4360.summary: So nature does not fail in necessary things for higher powers, because the perfections to which they are ordered cannot come from natural causes at all. Since lower beings' perfections do fall under such causality, nature would fail if it did not provide for them.
claims: Nature does not fail higher powers by not supplying what no natural cause could supply.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4385.summary: Reply to the third principal argument (regress): the possible intellect is disproportioned to firmly holding complex truths that cannot be known from phantasms and the agent intellect's natural light, that is, it is not proportionally movable by such agents. It is proportioned by something else: as mover, the supernatural revealer causing assent; and as form, the assent produced in it, a kind of inclination of the intellect toward that object.
claims: The intellect is disproportioned to certain complex truths relative to natural movers.
It is proportioned by a supernatural revealer as mover and by the caused assent as form.

jdso8u-d1e76-d1e4433.summary: Is that proportioning factor natural or supernatural? Supernatural, both as agent and as form. Is the intellect then disproportioned to it and in need of further proportioning? No: it is in obediential potency to the supernatural agent and so sufficiently proportioned to be moved by it; and being of itself capable of the assent so caused, it is naturally capable of receiving it. The regress stops at the second step: the revealed truth is not sufficiently inclining of itself, but the supernatural agent is, causing the assent that proportions the intellect, without any further proportioning.
claims: The proportioning agent and form are supernatural.
The intellect is in obediential potency to the supernatural agent and naturally capable of receiving the assent.
The regress stops because no further proportioning to the supernatural agent is needed.

jdso8u-d1e76.summary: Ordinatio I, Prologue part 1, q.1: whether in the present state man needs some supernaturally inspired doctrine he could not reach by the intellect's natural light. Scotus frames it as a dispute between philosophers, who affirm the perfection of nature, and theologians, who recognize its defect. Against the philosophers' arguments (agent and possible intellect as sufficient principles; the completeness of the speculative sciences; the virtual containment of all conclusions in first principles), he gives three arguments he judges probable: man cannot naturally know his end distinctly, with its conditions such as perpetuity and bodily resurrection; he cannot know the means, since beatitude comes through God's contingent acceptance of merits; and he cannot know what is proper to separate substances, above all God as triune and contingently causing, because we conceive them only in common concepts and effects mislead. Henry of Ghent's two further arguments are rejected. Scotus's solution distinguishes two senses of 'supernatural' (by agent, by supplying a supernatural object): simple concepts are naturally available via agent intellect and phantasm, but many necessary complex truths remain neutral to us and must be revealed by a supernatural agent who stands in for the divine essence as object, yielding obscure knowledge. God is man's natural end, attainable only supernaturally; the intellect has a natural passive capacity and obediential potency for this, which dignifies rather than disparages nature. Subsidiary discussions treat the salvation of the untaught (absolute versus ordained power, infused and acquired faith), the logic of descent under predicates, and the first object of the intellect, rejecting Avicenna's claim that being is naturally known as such.
claims: Supernaturally revealed doctrine is necessary for man in the present state.
Man cannot naturally know his end distinctly, the means to it, or the proper features of separate substances.
Beatitude follows from merit only through God's contingent acceptance.
Many necessary complex truths are neutral to natural reason and must be revealed.
Revelation is supernatural because its agent is not a natural mover and stands in for a supernatural object.
God is man's natural end, attainable only supernaturally.
First principles do not virtually contain all knowable conclusions.
By ordained power, grace is not infused without the habit of faith.
